note: Unscored review signals for post-release support risk (AQAF-057) and AI-assisted code (AQAF-058). They never change score or score_breakdown. Each states when it applies; a project it does not apply to is reported as not_applicable, not as lacking.

signals.name: Released software should keep a changelog or release notes
signals.applies: Projects that declare a publishable version (package.json, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml, a gemspec, composer.json) and have at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: CHANGELOG, HISTORY, NEWS or RELEASES file at the root, or a docs/releases or docs/changelog path.
signals.why: Without a record of what changed between versions, every upgrade question becomes a support request.
signals.remediation: Keep a CHANGELOG.md that lists user-visible changes per version, including breaking changes.

standards.title: Build, release, run
standards.note: strict separation of releases suggests keeping a record of each release

false_positive_classes: Release notes kept only on a hosting service (for example GitHub Releases), which a repository scan cannot see.
Changelog generated at publish time.

signals.name: Libraries and APIs should state a compatibility and deprecation policy
signals.applies: Profiles npm_library, php_package, ruby_gem or api_backend with at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: A mention of semantic versioning, deprecation or breaking changes in README, CHANGELOG, CONTRIBUTING or a docs Markdown file.
signals.why: Consumers cannot judge upgrade cost when the project never says what may change and how it signals removals.
signals.remediation: State the versioning scheme and how deprecations are announced, for example in the README or CHANGELOG.
signals.no_external_standard: compatibility policy is a release-management convention; none of the mapped standards defines it
false_positive_classes: Policy stated on a website outside the repository.
Policy implied by a version scheme such as calendar versioning.

signals.name: Large published libraries should ship migration or upgrade notes
signals.applies: Profiles npm_library, php_package, ruby_gem or api_backend with at least 50 code files.
signals.looks_for: A MIGRATION, UPGRADE or UPGRADING file, or a docs path with migration or upgrad in its name.
signals.why: Major-version upgrades are the usual point where consumers file support requests.
signals.remediation: Add MIGRATING.md or an upgrade section per major version.
signals.no_external_standard: no mapped standard defines upgrade notes
false_positive_classes: Projects still on their first major version.
Migration steps held inside the changelog.

signals.name: Applications should commit a dependency lockfile
signals.applies: Applications (not libraries) with a package.json, Cargo.toml with a binary, go.mod or a Python project, and at least 20 code files. Libraries are not asked: committing a lockfile for a library is debated.
signals.looks_for: package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, bun.lock, Cargo.lock, go.sum, poetry.lock, uv.lock, Pipfile.lock or a requirements file with pinned versions.
signals.why: Unpinned dependency resolution makes builds differ between machines and over time, which is hard to support after release.
signals.remediation: Commit the lockfile your package manager generates and install from it in CI.

standards.title: Pinned-Dependencies
standards.note: the Scorecard check recommends committing lock files for applications; the signal checks only that one exists

standards.title: Dependencies
standards.note: declare and isolate dependencies; a lockfile is one way to make that exact

false_positive_classes: Workspace or monorepo roots whose lockfile lives in a parent directory outside the scan.
Pinned versions in a requirements file the scanner does not parse.

signals.name: Larger projects should name their owners
signals.applies: Projects with at least 50 code files.
signals.looks_for: CODEOWNERS (root, .github or docs), MAINTAINERS, OWNERS, or an AUTHORS/GOVERNANCE file.
signals.why: When nobody is named, reviews and incident reports have no destination.
signals.remediation: Add a CODEOWNERS or MAINTAINERS file listing who answers for which area.

standards.title: Maintained
standards.note: the Scorecard check looks at recent activity, not at named owners; related only

false_positive_classes: Single-maintainer projects where the README names the maintainer.
Ownership recorded in a hosting-service team setting.

signals.name: Distributed software should publish a security policy
signals.applies: Projects that declare a publishable version and have at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: SECURITY.md (case-insensitive) at the root, in .github or in docs.
signals.why: Without a stated way to report a vulnerability, reports go to public issues or nowhere.
signals.remediation: Add SECURITY.md with a private reporting contact and the supported versions.

standards.title: Security-Policy
standards.note: the Scorecard Security-Policy check looks for a SECURITY.md file; this signal does the same

false_positive_classes: Organisation-wide policy inherited from a .github repository that the scan cannot see.

signals.name: Larger projects should state contribution rules
signals.applies: Projects with at least 50 code files.
signals.why: Contributors and agents guess at conventions when none are stated, which creates review churn.
signals.remediation: Add CONTRIBUTING.md covering how to build, test and submit a change.
signals.no_external_standard: contribution guides are a community convention; no mapped standard defines them
false_positive_classes: Projects that do not accept outside contributions.
Rules held in an organisation-level repository.

signals.name: Services should have runbook or operations notes
signals.applies: Profiles saas_or_web_app, api_backend, ai_pipeline or scraper_data_pipeline with at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: A RUNBOOK, OPERATIONS, DEPLOY, DEPLOYMENT, ONCALL or PLAYBOOK file, or a docs/runbook, docs/ops, docs/operations or docs/deploy path.
signals.why: Whoever supports the service after release needs to know how to start, check, roll back and diagnose it.
signals.remediation: Add a short runbook: how to deploy, how to check health, how to roll back, where logs go.

standards.title: Admin processes
standards.note: one-off admin tasks should be documented and repeatable; related background

false_positive_classes: Operations documentation kept in a wiki or another repository.
Internal prototypes with no operators.

signals.name: Services should expose a health or readiness signal
signals.applies: Profiles saas_or_web_app or api_backend with at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: The words health, healthz, readyz, readiness or liveness in code or deployment configuration.
signals.why: Orchestrators, load balancers and operators need a standard way to tell whether the service works.
signals.remediation: Add a health endpoint that checks the service can reach what it depends on.
signals.no_external_standard: no mapped standard defines a health endpoint
false_positive_classes: Health checks provided by a platform or sidecar outside the repository.
Frameworks that register health endpoints through configuration the scan does not read.

signals.name: Architecture should be described in a recognised form kept in the repository
signals.applies: Projects with at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: arc42 files or folders, ADR or MADR decision records (adr, adrs, decisions, doc/arch), C4 model files (workspace.dsl, *.c4, a c4 or structurizr folder), or an architecture document that cites one of these formats.
signals.why: A recognised format tells readers where to look and what is missing; free-form notes drift.
signals.remediation: Pick one format (for example ADRs for decisions and a short arc42 or C4 overview) and keep it next to the code.

standards.title: Architecture Decisions
standards.note: arc42 section 9 holds decisions; the signal only recognises that a known format is present

standards.title: Markdown Architectural Decision Records
standards.note: a common format for decision records

standards.title: C4 model
standards.note: a common notation for architecture diagrams

false_positive_classes: Architecture kept in a wiki or design tool outside the repository.
Documents in a recognised format with unusual file names.

signals.name: Repositories worked on with AI assistants should carry agent instructions
signals.applies: Projects with at least 20 code files.
signals.why: Assistants and agents guess at build commands, layout and rules when none are written down, and repeat the same mistakes.
signals.remediation: Add an AGENTS.md that states how to build and test, where code lives, and what must not change.
signals.no_external_standard: agent instruction files are a tooling convention; no mapped standard defines them
false_positive_classes: Projects not worked on with AI assistants.
Instructions kept in a user-level or organisation-level file outside the repository.

signals.name: Agent instructions should match the repository layout
signals.applies: Projects with an agent instruction file that names repository paths.
signals.looks_for: Backtick-quoted file and folder paths in the instruction files, checked against the scanned file list. Paths and bare names are also matched below any folder (crates, packages, apps); tokens without an extension whose first folder does not exist, hidden folders and node_modules are skipped; fewer than 2 unknown paths counts as consistent.
signals.why: Instructions that name files or folders that do not exist send agents to the wrong place and erode trust in the whole file.
signals.remediation: Update the instruction file when files move, or remove the stale paths.
signals.no_external_standard: no mapped standard covers agent instructions
false_positive_classes: Build outputs or generated folders (dist, build) that are ignored and so absent from the scan.
Paths that exist only after set-up, such as a local .env.
Paths in another repository of the same system.
Illustrative file names used as examples in the instructions (for example foo.ts).

signals.name: Tests should assert something
signals.applies: Projects with Python (test_*.py, *_test.py) or JavaScript/TypeScript (*.test.*, *.spec.*) test files.
signals.looks_for: Test files that define tests but contain no assert, expect, pytest.raises or equivalent.
signals.why: A test with no assertion passes whatever the code does, which gives false confidence during later changes.
signals.remediation: Add assertions that fail when the behaviour breaks, or delete the empty test.
signals.no_external_standard: test quality is not defined by the mapped standards
false_positive_classes: Smoke tests whose only check is that nothing throws.
Assertions made in shared helpers imported from another file.
Test frameworks with assertion styles the scanner does not recognise.

signals.name: Agent and prompt files should not hold secrets or internal endpoints
signals.applies: Projects with agent instruction, MCP, .cursor, .claude or prompt files.
signals.looks_for: Credential-like values (the AQ-CFG-001 precision rules) and internal hostnames or private-network URLs in those files. Values are never shown, only file names.
signals.why: Agent and prompt files are routinely committed, shared and sent to model providers, so secrets placed there leak.
signals.remediation: Move the value to the environment or a secret store and refer to it by name.

standards.title: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
standards.note: the signal looks for credential-like values, but only in agent and prompt files

false_positive_classes: Example or placeholder values the precision rules do not recognise.
Documented public endpoints on private-looking names.

signals.name: Source should not repeat large blocks between files
signals.applies: Projects with at least 20 code files.
signals.looks_for: Runs of 8 consecutive non-trivial lines that appear in more than one source file (at most 300 files, tests excluded). Fifty or more shared blocks counts as repetition; on a 300-repository sample the median count among repositories with any was 96, and the threshold is a guess, not calibrated.
signals.why: Generated code is often pasted rather than shared, so a fix has to be made in several places and one copy is missed.
signals.remediation: Extract the repeated block into a shared module and reuse it.
signals.no_external_standard: duplication is covered by general maintainability guidance, not by an item in the mapped standards
false_positive_classes: Generated or vendored source that is not in an ignored folder.
Boilerplate that a framework requires in every module.
Licence headers or repeated tables.
Mirrored copies kept by a sync or release script (for example vendored runtime copies of the same module).

signals.name: Declared Python dependencies should not look like misspelled popular packages
signals.applies: Projects that declare Python dependencies in requirements files or pyproject.toml. npm and other ecosystems are not covered.
signals.looks_for: Declared names that are not in a bundled, dated snapshot of the 8,000 most downloaded PyPI projects but differ from one by a single character (names of 7 or more characters). Everything else not in the snapshot is counted as unverified and not judged.
signals.why: Assistants sometimes invent or slightly misspell package names, and a squatted name can then be installed.
signals.remediation: Check each flagged name against the package index and correct the spelling.
signals.no_external_standard: no mapped standard defines a package-name check
false_positive_classes: Legitimate packages whose names differ by one character from a popular package.
Private or internal packages that happen to be near a public name.
Packages published after the snapshot date.
